opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that there's a lot of uncertainty, and I try to be upfront about that. When you're in an industry like this, the numbers don't behave like a normal business. Revenue has been growing very fast, something like an order of magnitude a year for a while, but nobody, including us, can promise that curve continues. So any projection of profitability in a particular year has wide error bars.

The way I think about it is that there are two big variables. The first is demand: how quickly models become economically useful enough that enterprises and individuals pay for them at scale. I'm fairly optimistic there, because we keep seeing the models get better at real work like coding, analysis, and agentic tasks, and adoption follows capability with a lag. The second is compute: how much we commit to spending on training and inference, and when. That's the hard part. You have to buy data center capacity a year or two in advance, based on guesses about what demand will look like. If you buy too little, you can't serve your customers and you fall behind. If you buy too much and the demand doesn't materialize on schedule, you can be in real financial trouble, even if you were right about the long-run picture and just wrong about the timing by a year.

So we try to be somewhat conservative. We don't want to bet the company on the most aggressive version of the curve. We try to plan so that if things go well we're in a strong position, and if growth is slower than expected we survive. That's a big part of why I'm careful about how much compute we commit to relative to some others in the industry.

Profitability in a given year is really a choice about how much to reinvest in the next generation of models. Every frontier lab could look more profitable by training less, but in a competitive environment that has costs. So when I talk about a target like 2028, I see it less as a precise forecast and more as a statement that the underlying unit economics work. Serving the models is profitable, and the question is how fast the scaling spending levels off relative to revenue. I think there's a reasonable path there, but I'd be lying if I said I was certain about the year.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that any projection like that has very wide error bars on it, and I want to be honest about that. When we put out a number like 2028, it's not a promise, it's a scenario. It comes out of a model with a bunch of inputs, and almost every one of those inputs is itself uncertain.

Let me try to break down where the uncertainty actually comes from, because I think people lump it all together and it's really several different things.

The first is demand. How fast does enterprise adoption of these models actually grow? We've seen revenue grow much faster than almost anyone predicted, including us. But that cuts both ways. If you'd asked me three years ago to forecast where we'd be today, I would have been off by a lot, in the optimistic direction as it turns out. So I have some humility about my ability to forecast three years forward. It could be faster, it could be slower.

The second is the cost structure, and that's really about compute. Training costs keep going up. Every generation of models costs more to train than the last one. The question is whether revenue from each generation grows faster than the cost of the next one. So far it has, but the relationship isn't guaranteed. If the scaling laws continue the way they have, and if inference costs keep falling the way they have, then the economics work out. If either of those bends, the picture changes.

The third thing, and this is the one I think is underappreciated, is that the whole thing is a bit of a race against your own investment. A company like ours could probably be profitable sooner if we chose to stop training frontier models. You'd just serve the models you have, collect the revenue, and you'd be a nice profitable business. But that would mean falling behind, and falling behind in this particular field, given what I think is at stake, isn't really an option for us. So the profitability date is partly a choice about how aggressively we keep investing, not purely something that happens to us.

And then there's the stuff you genuinely can't model. Regulation, geopolitics, what happens with export controls, whether some competitor decides to subsidize prices in a way that resets the whole market. Those are the fat tails.

So how do I think about it? I'd say I'm fairly confident in the direction. The business is real, the unit economics on inference are good and getting better, and the demand is clearly there. I'm much less confident about the precise year. If someone told me it ended up being 2027 or 2029 or 2030, I wouldn't be shocked by any of those. What I'd be more worried about is a world where the fundamental trend reversed, where the models stopped getting more useful per dollar spent. I don't think that's where we are, but that's the thing I actually watch, more than any specific date.

The way I'd put it to our own team is: the plan is a hypothesis, and we try to update it every quarter based on what we actually see rather than falling in love with the number.

astra-6.text:
I’d think of it as a conditional projection, rather than a precise prediction. There’s uncertainty on both sides: how quickly revenue grows, and how much we need to spend on training and serving the models. Those depend on technical progress, customer demand, and what it costs to deliver a given level of capability.

And those variables aren’t independent. If the technology improves faster, demand might grow faster, but we might also see a reason to invest more. So a later profitability date could reflect weaker business performance, or it could reflect a decision to pursue a larger opportunity. Those are very different situations.

I wouldn’t put too much weight on the exact year. The more useful question is whether the economics improve as the business scales, and how robust the plan is if growth or costs turn out differently than expected.
